articles.abstract: Norms are fundamental to social life, but basic questions about how they are affected by social context remain. Specifically, how do normative constraints depend on the presence and status of observers, and how do such relational contingencies vary across cultures? Using data from more than 25,000 individuals across 90 societies, we test several hypotheses linking normative constraints on everyday behaviors (like arguing, laughing, cursing, kissing, and crying), to the presence and status of observers. We find that behaviors widely viewed as appropriate in private become more constrained in the presence of others (an observer effect), and even more so when those others are higher in status (a status effect). Both observer and status effects are culturally universal, but the observer effect shows more variation across cultures. In particular, we find that observer effects are larger in societies that emphasize individualizing moral foundations, that is, avoiding harm and unfairness to others, because these societies are more permissive of actions when others are not around. The relative stability of status effects across cultural contexts suggests a universal tendency to defer in social hierarchies. These findings shed light on the relational contingency of everyday norms and underscore the role of such norms in the maintenance of social order and reproduction of inequality.

articles.title: Context disadvantage and residential mobility from early life into adulthood: impacts on socio-economic outcomes
articles.authors: Sergi Vidal, Maël Lecoursonnais, Riccardo Valente, Maria Brandén
articles.abstract: Individuals’ socio-economic trajectories are shaped by both persistence and change in their residential environments, making it essential to examine how the socio-spatial dynamics of context disadvantage and residential mobility interact over the life course. While prior research has often studied these factors separately and within specific life stages, less is known about their compound effects and their interrelatedness across childhood and adulthood. This study addresses this gap by investigating how exposure to residential contexts and residential mobility from birth influences socio-economic outcomes in early adulthood. Using Swedish longitudinal register data, we analyze residential trajectories and their association with economic and occupational (dis) advantage among individuals born between 1990 and 1993. Our findings show that mobility magnifies the associations between context exposure and socio-economic outcomes. Prolonged exposure to disadvantaged areas is most harmful when it coincides with moving, consistent with a compound penalty of instability and resource-poor environments. Second, moves in childhood are generally detrimental, while adult moves are opportunity-enhancing unless they occur in disadvantaged contexts, where the mobility premium levels off. Third, exiting disadvantaged contexts is associated with higher attainment than remaining persistently exposed, indicating that later socio-spatial trajectories can attenuate earlier disadvantage. These findings underscore the importance of considering both residential context and mobility across the life course for understanding—and interrupting—the reproduction of socio-economic inequality.

articles.title: One overworking breadwinner or two earners? Family economic standard of living by breadwinner arrangement, 1960 to 2018–2022
articles.abstract: Has the rise of rewards to long and inflexible work schedules altered the household-level economic viability of gendered divisions of paid work within marriage? This paper examines whether household arrangements centered on an overworking single breadwinner have become increasingly competitive, in terms of family economic standard of living, with non-overworking dual-breadwinner households. As prior research documents increasing rewards to overwork, particularly in professional and managerial occupations, overworking single-breadwinner families may have become economically competitive with dual-breadwinner households in which neither partner overworks. Using decennial Census and American Community Survey data from the Integrated Public Use Microdata Series covering 1960 to 2018–2022, we compare breadwinner arrangements across the income distribution and decompose changes in family income into changes in men’s earnings, women’s earnings, and non-labor income. Results show that overworking male- and female-breadwinner families experienced substantial relative gains at the top of the income distribution. Decomposition analyses indicate that these gains were driven primarily by accelerated earnings growth among overworking single breadwinners rather than earnings stagnation among dual earners. Although dual-breadwinner families with overworking breadwinners remain the most advantaged group, the gap between them and overworking single-breadwinner families narrowed substantially by 2018–2022. These findings suggest that labor market reward structures associated with long and inflexible work schedules may reshape family-level economic incentives in ways that reinforce gendered divisions of paid work, particularly among affluent families.

Generation Reunification, Generation COVID? Visualizing Formative Events in Germany
articles.abstract: Events and processes of social change experienced in the impressionable years can durably shape worldviews and attitudes throughout the life course. But which societal events do people experience as most defining? Drawing on responses to an open-ended question from an original probability-based online survey fielded in Germany in 2025, this data visualization shows that for older East Germans, the German reunification constituted an especially pivotal generational experience. For younger cohorts, by contrast, the COVID-19 pandemic was the most defining event, irrespective of political orientation, social status, and regional background. Immigration-related events, by contrast, matter mostly to politically right-leaning people. The authors demonstrate that the formative character of societal events is itself socially structured, shaped by region and political stance as much as by age.

articles.title: Quiet Quitting in America: An Empirical Assessment of Three Explanations
articles.abstract: Since 2022, quiet quitting has captured widespread public and scholarly attention, yet its causes remain poorly understood. This article advances the literature by identifying and empirically testing three explanations. Regression analyses using the 2014, 2018, and 2022 waves of the General Social Survey show that quiet quitting is more common among workers who enjoy better work environments and higher job satisfaction—contradicting the mainstream management explanation that portrays unhealthy environments and job dissatisfaction as the chief culprits. We also find that workers in more advantageous labor market positions and those permitted to work remotely are more likely to practice quiet quitting, supporting the a rational response explanation that conceptualizes workers as opportunistic actors with an inherent tendency to minimize effort. Consistent with the cultural shift explanation, workers who view work as an economic means rather than an intrinsically valuable activity are more likely to quietly quit, and the phenomenon has grown more prevalent in the postpandemic era. Together, these findings suggest that quiet quitting is not a new label for old problems addressable through managerial interventions but an emerging trend shaped by broader socioeconomic contexts. We conclude by discussing sociology’s crucial role in understanding quiet quitting and the underlying shifts in how individuals approach work in advanced capitalism.

articles.title: Bar Chart Looking Glass: How White Men Make Sense of Evidence Showing Intersectional Inequality in Their Profession
articles.abstract: Addressing long-standing inequalities in professions demands that professionals, especially those with power and privilege, believe that inequalities exist and are motivated to act. What promotes this inequality recognition? Focusing on an illustrative case of white, able-bodied, heterosexual men (WAHM) in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) fields, this study asks: How do these intersectionally advantaged professionals make sense of data illustrating inequality in their fields? Do they accept it as evidence of inequality or dismiss its legitimacy? What logics do they employ in their explanations? In interviews, we present a representative sample of 101 WAHM professionals with graphical evidence published in a generalist science journal showing patterns of intersectional inequality in respect and salary within U.S. STEM professions. A third of WAHM dismissed the epistemic legitimacy of one or both of these patterns outright. Even when WAHM acknowledged that group differences exist, only a third explained both respect and salary gaps as outcomes of systemic disadvantage. But seeing the data was transformative for some. We discuss the implications of these findings for equity advancement in STEM and beyond; they reveal that recognizing systemic group differences is not the same as recognizing inequalities in professions and that evidence alone will not convince advantaged professionals that inequalities exist.

articles.title: Panic on the Playground: The Distribution of Guns and Deadly Weapons in Indiana Schools
articles.abstract: Gun-related incidents in schools have captivated public attention and heavily influenced the organizational policies of K–12 education in the United States in recent decades. Using restricted administrative records of approximately 3 million students who ever attended public schools in the state of Indiana between 2006 and 2025, the authors analyze the prevalence and context of gun and deadly weapon events in schools. Although gun-related events are often assumed to be concentrated largely in urban and impoverished high schools, this visualization demonstrates that gun events occur across all school levels, as 25 percent of elementary schools, 41 percent of middle schools, and 52 percent of high schools report gun events over this period. This visualization also examines these trends by school poverty, highlighting that schools serving higher percentages of students in poverty report gun and deadly weapon events at higher rates. However, schools serving lower percentages of students in poverty are far from immune from weapon events.
